title: Transgender Athletes & Equal Protection
hook: Can a state law treat male and female athletes differently and still satisfy the Constitution's promise of equal treatment? In 2026 the Supreme Court said yes, for school sports.
key_points: The Equal Protection Clause requires government to justify laws that classify people by sex.
Sex-based classifications generally get 'intermediate scrutiny': the law must serve an important goal and be substantially related to it.
Several states passed laws barring transgender girls and women from girls' and women's school sports teams.
In June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled such laws are constitutionally permitted, per SCOTUSblog.
The case shows how equal-protection doctrine, not just policy debate, decides where a sex-based line can legally be drawn.
content_html: Not every law that treats people differently is unconstitutional — but a law that classifies people by sex has to clear a real legal hurdle. Under the Equal Protection Clause, courts generally apply "intermediate scrutiny" to sex-based classifications: the government must show the law serves an important objective and that the sex-based line is substantially related to achieving it.
extra_html: That doctrine was at the center of a wave of state laws restricting transgender girls and women from competing on girls' and women's school sports teams — and of the litigation those laws provoked, since opponents argued the classifications fail equal-protection scrutiny while supporters argued they satisfy it by protecting competitive fairness in sex-separated sports. According to SCOTUSblog's Amy Howe, the Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 that states may enforce such exclusions. Whatever one's view of the underlying policy, the case is a clear illustration of how equal-protection doctrine actually functions: it doesn't ban sex-based rules outright, it asks courts to weigh the government's stated purpose against the classification drawn — and where that balance lands can shift as courts revisit it. (This card describes U.S. constitutional doctrine specifically; other countries and sports bodies set eligibility rules through very different processes.)

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

flashcards.prompt: What legal test do courts generally apply to laws that classify people by sex?
flashcards.back_html: "Intermediate scrutiny": the government must show the law serves an important objective and that the sex-based classification is substantially related to it.

No state may regulate school sports eligibility

choices.text: Courts weigh the government's stated purpose against the sex-based classification, rather than banning such laws outright
